Bedside screen (qSOFA): two or more of respiratory rate 22 or more, altered mentation, systolic blood pressure 100 or less.
Pulse pressure = systolic blood pressure minus diastolic blood pressure.

snip.t: 1. *Shock:* Systolic blood pressure <90 mmHg, pallor, cold extremities, diaphoresis.
Pulsus paradoxus: An exaggerated inspiratory drop in systolic blood pressure (>10 mmHg).
Persistent resting tachycardia, hypotension (systolic blood pressure <90 mmHg), or refractory fluid overload.

Vasodilators: If systolic blood pressure remains adequate, start an intravenous nitrate infusion (glyceryl trinitrate) to unload the left ventricle by reducing systemic vascular resistance and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure.
Hypotension: Systolic blood pressure $<90\text{ mmHg}$ or mean arterial pressure $<65\text{ mmHg}$ indicates failure of compensatory vasoconstriction to offset low stroke volume or vasodilation.

qs.q: A clinical investigator wants to verify whether patient systolic blood pressure readings follow a normal distribution curve before running parametric tests. Which specialized graphical diagnostic tool should be generated?
o: Bivariate regression curve.
Cumulative frequency polygon.
Categorical box whisker.
Simple error bar.
Probability probability plot.
qs.e: P-P plots visually assess how closely a dataset's distribution matches a theoretical normal distribution.

qs.q: A 60-year-old man with a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm is brought into the resuscitation bay with a systolic blood pressure of 72 mmHg. The trauma team decides on a strategy of permissive hypotension. Which physiological alteration is primarily responsible for preventing further clot disruption under this regimen?
o: Decreasing sheer stress forces acting directly upon fragile developing thrombi
Elevating systemic peripheral resistance to limit total intravascular loss
Lowering cardiac stroke output variables to reduce central venous pressure
Suppressing endogenous catecholamine surges that destabilize vessel walls
Minimizing mechanical pulse wave pressures that dislodge sealing plugs
qs.e: Lower pressure reduces mechanical disruption of fragile early hemostatic plugs at injury sites.

qs.q: A 42-year-old male is admitted following a motor vehicle collision with multiple long-bone fractures and a systolic blood pressure of 82 mmHg. The resuscitation team initiates a 1:1:1 ratio massive transfusion protocol. What is the rationale for maintaining this specific fixed ratio of blood products?
o: Replicating whole blood composition to prevent dilutional coagulopathy
Maximizing red cell mass delivery while minimizing total volume
Providing adequate platelet counts to overcome ongoing endothelial injury
Preventing severe citrate toxicity through balanced calcium delivery
Restoring oncotic pressure rapidly without risking pulmonary edema
qs.e: A 1:1:1 ratio of plasma, platelets, and RBCs mimics whole blood to treat and prevent dilutional coagulopathy.

qs.q: A 22-year-old victim of a knife assault has an initial systolic blood pressure of 88 mmHg in the emergency department. The attending surgeon advises against pushing normal saline bolus infusions. What pathological cascade is primarily being avoided?
o: Dilution of clotting factors and worsening hypothermia
Direct osmotic injury to renal tubular basement membranes
Severe pulmonary edema from capillary leak syndrome
Systemic vasoconstriction leading to organ ischemia
Electrolyte shifts provoking fatal cardiac arrhythmias
qs.e: Aggressive crystalloid resuscitation dilutes existing coagulation factors and exacerbates bleeding through hypothermia and clot disruption.

qs.q: A 32-year-old man involved in a motor vehicle collision presents with a penetrating abdominal injury and active haemorrhage. His systolic blood pressure is 85 mmHg and mean arterial pressure is 55 mmHg. What is the primary clinical rationale for avoiding immediate aggressive crystalloid normalisation of his blood pressure?
o: To prevent disruption of an immature platelet-fibrin clot
To ensure complete cessation of bleeding without surgery
To eliminate the risk of transfusion-related acute lung injury
To maintain normal renal perfusion and prevent kidney failure
qs.e: Permissive hypotension avoids high pressure that can disrupt early clots and dilute coagulation factors. It is a temporary bridge, not a definitive replacement for surgical control.

qs.q: An adult trauma patient without a traumatic brain injury is being managed with hypotensive resuscitation while awaiting emergency laparotomy for an intra-abdominal bleed. Which of the following represents the commonly cited temporary systolic blood pressure target?
o: Target a temporary systolic blood pressure of 60 to 70 mmHg
Target a temporary systolic blood pressure of 100 to 110 mmHg
Target a temporary systolic blood pressure of 120 to 130 mmHg
Target a temporary systolic blood pressure of 80 to 90 mmHg
qs.e: In selected adult trauma patients without traumatic brain injury, the commonly cited temporary SBP target is approximately 80-90 mmHg. Higher pressures may worsen bleeding before definitive control.

ai.title: Systolic Blood Pressure in Clinical Assessment
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Systolic blood pressure (SBP) is the key bedside vital for assessing perfusion, shock, and cardiovascular risk. Understanding its measurement, interpretation, and limits is essential for acute and chronic care, especially where resources are limited.

sections.p: SBP is the peak arterial pressure during left‑ventricular systole, measured with a cuff or invasive line. Normal adult range is 90–120 mmHg; values <90 mmHg define hypotension.
b: Measured at the brachial artery with a calibrated cuff
Invasive arterial line gives continuous SBP in critically ill patients

sections.p: SBP guides shock staging and hypertension grading. In shock, SBP <90 mmHg signals decompensation; in hypertension, SBP 140–159 mmHg is Stage 1, 160–179 mmHg Stage 2, ≥180 mmHg Stage 3.
b: Hypotension: SBP <90 mmHg or MAP <65 mmHg
Hypertension stages follow WHO/ISH thresholds

sections.p: Low SBP results from reduced stroke volume, vasodilation, or impaired cardiac output. In low‑resource settings, common precipitants include severe malaria, septicemia (often from typhoid or TB), hemorrhage (e.g., obstetric), and cardiac disease (rheumatic heart disease, pericardial tamponade).
b: Hypovolemia – diarrhoea, vomiting, obstetric bleed
Septic shock – malaria, bacterial sepsis, TB meningitis
Cardiogenic shock – rheumatic valve disease, myocardial infarction
Distributive shock – anaphylaxis, neurogenic injury

sections.p: Patients with low SBP appear pale, cold, and diaphoretic; mental status may be altered. A narrow pulse pressure (<30 mmHg) suggests low stroke volume, while a wide pulse pressure (>60 mmHg) can indicate aortic regurgitation or sepsis.
b: Cold extremities, delayed capillary refill
Altered mentation (confusion, lethargy)
Tachycardia compensates until decompensation

t.b: What is the current SBP? – Determines need for urgent resuscitation
Is there intra‑abdominal bleeding? – Guides fluid vs. surgical intervention
Is tissue hypoperfusion present? – Elevated >2 mmol/L supports shock
Are electrolytes and renal function stable? – Guides fluid choice

t.a: If cuff unavailable, palpation of radial pulse and capillary refill
t.b: Is perfusion adequate? – Provides crude assessment when equipment lacking

sections.p: Sustained SBP <90 mmHg leads to organ ischemia, acute kidney injury, myocardial infarction, and death. In hypertensive emergencies, SBP ≥180 mmHg with end‑organ damage (e.g., encephalopathy) requires rapid control.
b: Altered consciousness
Chest pain or ECG changes
Oliguria <0.5 mL/kg/h
Cool, mottled skin despite fluids

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then restore perfusion. Fluid resuscitation (crystalloids 20 mL/kg) is first‑line for hypovolemic shock; vasopressors (e.g., norepinephrine) are added if SBP remains <90 mmHg after fluids. In distributive shock, early antibiotics for sepsis are critical. Avoid excessive nitroglycerin in hypotension; use only when SBP >100 mmHg and pulmonary edema is present.
b: IV crystalloids 20 mL/kg bolus
Norepinephrine infusion if SBP <90 mmHg after fluids
Treat infection: broad‑spectrum antibiotics, malaria antimalarials
Control bleeding surgically or with uterotonics
Monitor urine output, mental status, and repeat SBP

sections.p: After stabilization, identify and modify precipitating factors: treat chronic infections (TB, HIV), ensure safe obstetric care, educate on malaria prophylaxis, and manage chronic hypertension to avoid future crises.
b: Schedule repeat vitals every 15 min until stable
Arrange definitive source control (e.g., surgery, antibiotics)
Counsel on fluid intake, malaria nets, and antenatal care

sections.p: Pulse pressure abnormalities can be mistaken for SBP problems. A low pulse pressure may be misread as isolated hypotension, but it actually reflects low stroke volume.
b: Pulse pressure vs. SBP alone
Mean arterial pressure (MAP) – MAP = DBP + 1/3 pulse pressure

sections.p: In severe anemia, SBP may appear normal despite poor oxygen delivery. Conversely, a high SBP in early septic shock can mask underlying tissue hypoperfusion.
b: Normal SBP with high lactate → occult shock
White‑coat hypertension → over‑treatment

whenToSeekHelp: SBP <90 mmHg with altered mental status
Chest pain or new ECG changes

faq.q: Why can a patient have normal SBP but still be in shock?
faq.a: Compensated shock maintains SBP via tachycardia and vasoconstriction; tissue hypoxia is revealed by lactate or mental changes.

faq.q: What is the significance of a pulse pressure >60 mmHg?
faq.a: It suggests high stroke volume or vasodilation, common in sepsis or aortic regurgitation.

faq.q: When should I start a vasopressor?
faq.a: If SBP remains <90 mmHg after 1–2 fluid boluses and signs of poor perfusion persist.

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman in labour suddenly collapses with SBP 78 mmHg – what immediate steps and why? — Assess airway, give 20 mL/kg crystalloid, consider uterine massage and oxytocin, prepare for blood transfusion; SBP <90 mmHg signals hypovolemic shock.

A patient with severe malaria has SBP 95 mmHg but lactate 4 mmol/L – how do you interpret? — Normal SBP may mask early septic shock; elevated lactate indicates tissue hypoxia, prompting aggressive fluids and antimalarials.

Why is norepinephrine preferred over dopamine in septic shock in low‑resource settings? — Norepinephrine reliably raises SBP with fewer arrhythmias; dopamine’s dose‑dependent effects increase risk of tachyarrhythmia and renal vasoconstriction.
How does pulsus paradoxus help differentiate cardiac tamponade from hypovolemia? — An inspiratory SBP drop >10 mmHg suggests tamponade; hypovolemia lacks this exaggerated drop.

A hypertensive patient presents with SBP 190 mmHg and headache – what urgent management is needed? — Identify end‑organ damage; if present, start IV labetalol or nicardipine, aiming for SBP <160 mmHg within 1 hour.
What are the limitations of using qSOFA in a malaria‑endemic clinic? — qSOFA relies on SBP ≤100 mmHg, which may be normal early in malaria; missing early shock leads to delayed treatment.

Explain why a wide pulse pressure can be misleading in a septic patient with SBP 120 mmHg. — High SBP may hide low systemic vascular resistance; pulse pressure >60 mmHg indicates vasodilation despite apparently normal SBP.
When is it unsafe to give nitroglycerin to a patient with acute pulmonary edema? — If SBP <100 mmHg, nitroglycerin can precipitate hypotension and worsen organ perfusion.
